It explicitly portrays the experienced elders (זְקֵנִים) offering wise, merciful counsel to King Rehoboam, while the young elite counselors give harsh, foolish advice that leads to national division. Rehoboam's rejection of the elders' counsel in favor of the young men's strategy ('my little finger is thicker than my father's loins') results in disaster and rebellion by the common people. Additionally, Jeroboam himself—initially just a servant (עֶבֶד), not elite by birth—is divinely chosen as king, suggesting that status does not determine capability or worthiness. The text demonstrates through these examples that elite status does not confer inherent superiority in judgment or wisdom.
